Let G be a directed graph. Define the transitive closure GT as the directed
graph sharing the same vertex set as G, where an edge u →v exists in GT if and only if
there is a directed path from u to v in G. Furthermore, define a transitive reduction of G to
be a graph with the minimum number of edges such that its transitive closure is identical to
GT. Given that a graph may generally admit multiple transitive reductions, prove that G
possesses a unique transitive reduction if and only if G is acyclic.
Theorem 1. Let G be a directed graph. Then G possesses a unique transitive reduction if
and only if G is acyclic.
Proof. We prove both directions of the equivalence.
(⇒) If G is acyclic, then G has a unique transitive reduction.
Assume G is acyclic. Since G is acyclic, its transitive closure GT is also acyclic (as paths
in G cannot create cycles).
Define the relation:
R = {(u, v) ∈GT : ∄w ̸= u, v such that (u, w) ∈GT and (w, v) ∈GT}
That is, R consists of all edges in GT that cannot be obtained by composing two other
edges via transitivity.
Lemma 1. The graph R defined above satisfies RT = GT.
Proof of Lemma. Since R ⊆GT by construction, we have RT ⊆GT.
For the reverse inclusion, let (u, v) ∈GT. We prove (u, v) ∈RT by strong induction on
the length of the shortest path from u to v in G.
Base case: If the shortest path has length 1, then (u, v) is a direct edge in G, hence in
GT. Moreover, there is no intermediate vertex w with paths u →w →v, so (u, v) ∈R, and
thus (u, v) ∈RT.
Inductive step: Suppose the shortest path from u to v in G has length k > 1. If (u, v) ∈R,
we are done. Otherwise, there exists w ̸= u, v with (u, w), (w, v) ∈GT. The shortest paths
from u to w and from w to v have lengths strictly less than k (since G is acyclic). By the
inductive hypothesis, (u, w), (w, v) ∈RT. Therefore, (u, v) ∈RT by transitivity.
Lemma 2. R has the minimum number of edges among all graphs with transitive closure
GT.
Proof of Lemma. Suppose R′ is any graph with R′T = GT. We show |R′| ≥|R|.
For any (u, v) ∈R, by definition there is no intermediate vertex w such that (u, w), (w, v) ∈
GT. This means any path from u to v in GT must include the direct edge (u, v).
Since R′T = GT, there must be a path from u to v in R′. If (u, v) /∈R′, then this path
must go through some intermediate vertex w′ with (u, w′) ∈R′T and (w′, v) ∈R′T. But
since R′T = GT, we have (u, w′), (w′, v) ∈GT, contradicting the definition of (u, v) ∈R.
Therefore, (u, v) ∈R′ for all (u, v) ∈R, which implies |R′| ≥|R|.
Lemma 3. R is the unique transitive reduction.
Proof of Lemma. From the previous lemmas, R is a transitive reduction.
Suppose R′ is
another transitive reduction with |R′| = |R| and R′T = GT.
From the proof of Lemma 2, we showed R ⊆R′. Since |R| = |R′|, we have R = R′.
